title: The One With The Ballroom Dancing

jokes.text: The old condom ring in the leather just doesn't say 'cool' anymore.
jokes.setup: Someone asks about Chandler's new wallet, and he says 'it was time'
jokes.punchline: The old condom ring in the leather just doesn't say 'cool' anymore — implying the condom was so long unused it permanently embossed his wallet
jokes.explanation: A sharp cold-open joke perfectly calibrated to Chandler's self-deprecating voice. The detail — the condom ring worn into the leather — implies he hasn't had sex in so long the condom left a permanent impression. It's economical, specific, and only Chandler would frame his own sexlessness as a 'cool' metric. Strong opener.

dialogue.speaker: Joey
dialogue.line: My wallet was getting worn out. There was this ring worn into the leather from carrying a condom around so much.

dialogue.speaker: Chandler
dialogue.line: A condom ring? Joey, that's not a real thing.

dialogue.speaker: Joey
dialogue.line: It is too! Look, see? It's right here. And now it's permanently imprinted. The wallet's ruined. It's not cool anymore.

jokes.text: Rachel puts an empty carton back in the fridge. Monica calls her out. Rachel: 'I know, but the garbage was full.'
jokes.setup: Monica points out Rachel put an empty carton back in the fridge
jokes.punchline: Rachel's logic: the garbage was full, so the fridge is a valid alternative
jokes.explanation: A solid character joke that plays on Rachel's entitled obliviousness. The logic is absurd but internally consistent — she knew it was empty, she just didn't care. Character-integrated, functional sitcom comedy.

dialogue.speaker: Monica
dialogue.line: Rachel, you can't just put an empty container back in the fridge!

dialogue.speaker: Rachel
dialogue.line: Why not? I'm not using it.

dialogue.speaker: Monica
dialogue.line: Because the next person thinks there's food in there!

dialogue.speaker: Rachel
dialogue.line: Well, there was when I put it back.

jokes.text: Monica asks Rachel if she has ever taken out the trash since she's lived there. Rachel: 'Well, I thought you liked doing it.'
jokes.setup: Monica escalates — has Rachel EVER taken out the trash?
jokes.punchline: Rachel genuinely thought Monica liked doing it — pure entitled obliviousness played straight
jokes.explanation: The escalation from the previous joke lands well. Rachel's genuine belief that Monica enjoys taking out trash is a perfect encapsulation of her character's pre-growth obliviousness. Slightly predictable but well-executed.

dialogue.speaker: Rachel
dialogue.line: Well, maybe if Monica actually did her chores around here, I'd have time to replace the milk!

jokes.text: Treeger's escalating list of princess demands: 'Daddy, buy me a pizza. Daddy, buy me a candy factory. Daddy, make the cast of Cats sing Happy Birthday to me.'
jokes.setup: Treeger sarcastically mocks Rachel as a spoiled princess
jokes.punchline: The demands escalate absurdly — from pizza to a candy factory to having the cast of Cats perform for her birthday
jokes.explanation: A well-structured escalation joke. The third beat — the cast of Cats singing Happy Birthday — is the right level of absurd specificity. 'Cats' in particular is a great choice: it's theatrical, ridiculous, and very specific. The rule of three is executed cleanly.

dialogue.speaker: Monica
dialogue.line: Rachel, when was the last time you took out the trash?

dialogue.speaker: Rachel
dialogue.line: I don't know, like... last week?

dialogue.speaker: Monica
dialogue.line: Rachel, it's been two months.

dialogue.speaker: Rachel
dialogue.line: Well, I just assumed you liked doing it. You're always so... organized.

jokes.text: Treeger: 'God, if you're going to cry about it!' — Treeger storms off disgusted after making Rachel cry.
jokes.setup: Treeger has been berating Rachel; the confrontation has made Rachel actually cry.
jokes.punchline: Treeger, clearly the one who caused the crying, acts disgusted that she's crying — the aggressor appalled at the victim's reaction.
jokes.explanation: The irony of Treeger being disgusted by crying he caused is functional but not particularly original. It works as a button on the scene.

dialogue.speaker: Rachel
dialogue.line: I don't come to the trash room often.

dialogue.speaker: Treeger
dialogue.line: Oh no, what a shock. A princess like you in the trash room.

jokes.text: Joey: 'Treeger made you cry?' Rachel: 'He said really mean things that were only partly true.'
jokes.setup: Joey asks what happened with Treeger
jokes.punchline: Rachel's qualifier — 'only partly true' — admits the insults had merit while trying to save face
jokes.explanation: A very sharp line. The 'only partly true' admission is self-aware in exactly the right way — Rachel knows the princess critique landed because it was accurate, but she can't fully concede. Economical and perfectly in character.

dialogue.speaker: Treeger
dialogue.line: You know what your problem is? You're spoiled.

dialogue.speaker: Treeger
dialogue.line: First you want pizza, then you want candy from a candy factory, now you want to go to a Broadway show? What's next, you want me to get you the moon?

dialogue.speaker: Rachel
dialogue.line: Well, actually, I was thinking more along the lines of Cats.

jokes.text: Joey: 'All right, that's it. School is in session!' — then reveals he's showing Chandler a gym card.
jokes.setup: Joey dramatically announces 'school is in session' after declaring he'll teach Treeger a lesson
jokes.punchline: The dramatic setup implies Joey has a plan to deal with Treeger; instead he produces a gym card and starts talking about quitting the gym
jokes.explanation: Mild misdirection that pivots the scene. The comedic deflation is functional but not particularly sharp. The gym card pivot is more of a scene transition device than a true punchline.

dialogue.speaker: Treeger
dialogue.line: What? I'm just saying, you're always leaving your door open. It's a security risk.

dialogue.speaker: Rachel
dialogue.line: Well maybe I like leaving my door open!

dialogue.speaker: Treeger
dialogue.line: Oh, come on. You're gonna cry about this?

jokes.text: Ross pulls out his gym card and reveals he's missed 'the last 1,200 times.'
jokes.setup: Ross finds a gym card and mentions he tries to go four times a week.
jokes.punchline: He's missed the last 1,200 times — a specific, absurdly large number that implies he hasn't gone in years.
jokes.explanation: The specificity of 1,200 makes it funnier than a vague 'a lot.' Good structure — the setup of '4 times a week' makes the math of 1,200 even more damning. Clean, efficient comedy.

dialogue.speaker: Rachel
dialogue.line: He said I was selfish and superficial, and okay, maybe I am a *little* selfish and *a lot* superficial, but that doesn't mean he gets to say it!

jokes.text: Chandler: 'I try to go four times a week, but I've missed... the last 1200 times.'
jokes.setup: Chandler claims to be a gym member who tries to go four times a week
jokes.punchline: 'The last 1200 times' — the pause before the number and the specificity of 1200 make it hit
jokes.explanation: The specificity of '1200' is the key craft element — it's not a round number, which makes it funnier and implies Chandler has actually done the math on his own failure. The pause implied by the ellipsis in the transcript heightens it. Chandler's self-deprecating voice is perfectly deployed.

dialogue.speaker: Rachel
dialogue.line: Just forget about the Treeger incident, okay?

dialogue.speaker: Joey
dialogue.line: Forget about it? Rachel, I was almost killed! The man came at me with a wrench. A wrench! Do you know what a wrench can do to a face? A beautiful face like this?

jokes.text: Chandler: 'You think I like having $50 a month taken from my account? They make you go all the way down there. They use all these phrases and peppiness to confuse you.'
jokes.setup: Joey asks why Chandler doesn't just quit the gym
jokes.punchline: Chandler describes quitting the gym as if the gym is a hostile institution that uses psychological warfare ('phrases and peppiness') to trap members
jokes.explanation: 'Phrases and peppiness' is a good, specific comic phrase. The conspiracy-like framing of a gym's sales tactics is relatable and mildly clever. Sets up the Maria payoff well.

dialogue.speaker: Joey
dialogue.line: Treeger, you are like a teacher. You taught me everything I know. And now... now I have to use what you taught me against you.

jokes.text: Chandler: 'And then they bring out Maria.' Joey: 'Who is Maria?' Chandler: 'Oh, Maria!' — with reverent dread
jokes.setup: Chandler is explaining why he can't quit the gym
jokes.punchline: The way Chandler says 'Oh, Maria!' — with implied awe/helplessness — is the joke: a grown man rendered powerless by a gym salesperson
jokes.explanation: The call-and-response structure (Joey's naïve question, Chandler's reverent 'Oh, Maria!') is a nice bit of comic escalation through tone rather than content. Sets up the gym subplot effectively.

dialogue.speaker: Chandler
dialogue.line: I haven't been to the gym in so long, they're charging me for 1200 missed sessions.

jokes.text: Chandler: 'She's like this lycra, spandex-covered gym treat.'
jokes.setup: Chandler is explaining Maria's power over him
jokes.punchline: 'Gym treat' — an absurdly clinical and mild phrase to describe someone Chandler clearly finds irresistible
jokes.explanation: 'Gym treat' is a wonderfully deflated phrase — the contrast between lycra/spandex (suggestive) and 'treat' (like a pet snack) is pure Chandler. Good economy and character voice.

dialogue.speaker: Chandler
dialogue.line: I can't quit the gym. Every time I try to quit, she uses the same line on me. She goes, 'But you've lost three pounds!' And I'm like, 'Really?' And I stay.

dialogue.speaker: Chandler
dialogue.line: It's like Jedi mind tricks. She's a Jedi. 'These are not the fries you're looking for.'

jokes.text: Joey offers to come hold Chandler's hand at the gym. Chandler: 'You're strong enough to face her?' Joey: 'Oh, no. You'll have to come.'
jokes.setup: Joey offers to help Chandler face Maria
jokes.punchline: Joey's bravado collapses immediately — he asks if Chandler is strong enough, and when pressed, admits HE isn't strong enough either
jokes.explanation: Joey's immediate reversal is characteristically funny — he appoints himself the strong one, then reveals he's just as weak. Good use of Joey's overconfident-but-clueless voice.

dialogue.speaker: Chandler
dialogue.line: She's like a gym treat. You know, you work out, you get all sweaty, and then you go get a little treat.

dialogue.speaker: Joey
dialogue.line: What are you talking about?

dialogue.speaker: Chandler
dialogue.line: I'm saying she's what you'd want to have after working out. Like, the perfect reward. Except she wears so much lycra, it's like trying to unwrap a very athletic candy bar.

jokes.text: Joey confronts Treeger: 'Maybe you haven't heard of not making girls cry.' Treeger: 'Maybe you haven't heard of the Rent Stabilization Act of 1968.'
jokes.setup: Joey tries to intimidate Treeger with vague moral authority about making Rachel cry
jokes.punchline: Treeger counters with hyper-specific legal knowledge that completely deflates Joey's bluster
jokes.explanation: This is one of the episode's strongest jokes. The structural contrast is perfect: Joey's vague, pompous moral claim ('haven't heard of not making girls cry') vs. Treeger's precise, devastating legal counter. The specificity of '1968' is key — it makes the joke feel real and authoritative. Joey being out-intimidated by legalese is excellent character comedy. Joey's follow-up admission ('I have actually not heard of that') seals it perfectly.

dialogue.speaker: Joey
dialogue.line: Tribbiani!

dialogue.speaker: Treeger
dialogue.line: What? Another leak?

jokes.text: Joey: 'I have actually not heard of that.'
jokes.setup: Treeger invokes the Rent Stabilization Act of 1968 as his counter-threat
jokes.punchline: Joey's honest admission that he has not, in fact, heard of that — delivered with complete sincerity
jokes.explanation: The tag to joke 13 is almost as good as the joke itself. Joey's sincere, undefensive acknowledgment that Treeger's legal knowledge has stumped him is perfectly in character. The economy is exceptional — five words that completely puncture the scene's tension.

dialogue.speaker: Joey
dialogue.line: Listen to me, I'm gonna tell you something. There's a law, okay? It's called the 'You Make a Girl Cry, You're a Bad Guy' law. Look it up!

jokes.text: Phoebe: 'My first massage is this incredibly gorgeous guy. Every time I see him, I want to do things to him I can't charge for.'
jokes.setup: Phoebe complains about her first massage client of the day
jokes.punchline: 'Things I can't charge for' — a euphemism that implies sexual attraction while inverting the usual worry (the client's safety) onto Phoebe's professional restraint
jokes.explanation: The phrase 'things I can't charge for' is a clever euphemism that implies both the illegal-massage-parlor joke and Phoebe's genuine infatuation. Good economy and character voice — Phoebe's guileless delivery makes it land.

dialogue.speaker: Joey
dialogue.line: You can't do this! I know my rights!

dialogue.speaker: Treeger
dialogue.line: Oh yeah? Well according to section 4, subsection B of the New York Housing Maintenance Code, I can do whatever I want.

jokes.text: Monica: 'They make you take an oath?' Phoebe: 'No, I made myself take one. No fooling around with clients... and always be prepared. That one's from the Boy Scouts, but it just makes good sense.'
jokes.setup: Phoebe mentions her oath as a masseuse
jokes.punchline: Her personal oath mixes a legitimate professional rule with the Boy Scout motto — and she defends the latter as universally practical wisdom
jokes.explanation: A quintessential Phoebe joke. She invented her own oath, borrowed a Boy Scout motto, and her completely earnest defense of it ('it just makes good sense') is perfectly in character. The logic is absurd but Phoebe-internally-consistent. Strong character integration.

dialogue.speaker: Joey
dialogue.line: I have no idea what you're talking about.

jokes.text: Rachel notices Phoebe's new ankle bracelet and pedicure: 'Your feet are all dressed up.' Then: 'That's the only part he can see when he's on the table!'
jokes.setup: Rachel notices Phoebe's ankle bracelet and pedicure and compliments her 'dressed up feet'
jokes.punchline: The reason is revealed — it's the only body part her client Rick can see during a massage. Phoebe is flirting via foot presentation.
jokes.explanation: The comedic insight — that Phoebe has been doing 'foot flirting' — is genuinely funny and original for the show. 'Your feet are all dressed up' is a charming phrase, and the reveal of Phoebe's logic (foot presentation as the only flirting avenue) is absurd but coherent.

dialogue.speaker: Joey
dialogue.line: Yeah, well, I already knew that.

jokes.text: Monica: 'You're going to do some feet flirting!' Phoebe: 'I don't know what you're talking about.' Monica: 'How do you explain the toe ring?' Phoebe: 'It's Arabian Princess Day at work. Leave me alone!'
jokes.setup: Monica accuses Phoebe of 'feet flirting'; Phoebe denies it
jokes.punchline: 'It's Arabian Princess Day at work. Leave me alone!' — an invented, utterly implausible excuse delivered with complete conviction
jokes.explanation: One of the episode's best jokes. 'Arabian Princess Day at work' is a perfect Phoebe excuse — it's specific enough to sound like she thought about it, absurd enough to be obviously false, and delivered with the defensive energy of someone who knows they've been caught. The 'Leave me alone!' tag prevents it from over-explaining. Only Phoebe could deliver this. Comparable to classic Phoebe non-sequiturs.

dialogue.speaker: Phoebe
dialogue.line: Oh my God, this guy came in today, and he was so gorgeous. Like, seriously, the most beautiful man I've ever seen.

dialogue.speaker: Phoebe
dialogue.line: And he wanted a full body massage, so I was like, 'Oh yeah, I can definitely help you with that.'

dialogue.speaker: Phoebe
dialogue.line: And then he asked if I do any... special services. And I was like, 'Well, that depends on what you're looking for.'

dialogue.speaker: Phoebe
dialogue.line: So he says, 'What's your rate for a happy ending?' And I told him my rates are very competitive.

jokes.text: Joey returns from Treeger with the news. Rachel: 'You got us evicted?' Joey: 'I told you not to go down there.' Rachel: 'He made Rachel cry!' Joey (as Chandler): 'Rachel always cries!'
jokes.setup: Joey tried to defend Rachel's honor and instead got them threatened with eviction
jokes.punchline: The argument escalates to Joey's defense ('He made Rachel cry!') being countered with 'Rachel always cries!' — a true and slightly mean observation
jokes.explanation: The 'Rachel always cries' line is accurate-but-brutal in a funny way. Chandler's willingness to say it out loud is good character comedy. Functional sitcom argument scene.

dialogue.speaker: Phoebe
dialogue.line: Oh, I made up my own oath. It's like, 'I swear to be professional and keep my clients' bodies and secrets safe, to always be prepared, and to do a good turn daily.'

jokes.text: Monica: 'You go down there and you suck up to him. You suck like you've never sucked before!'
jokes.setup: Monica orders Joey to go apologize to Treeger
jokes.punchline: The instruction 'suck up' becomes 'suck like you've never sucked before' — the double meaning isn't quite a pun but the escalating enthusiasm of the phrasing is inherently funny
jokes.explanation: The line works on Monica's intensity and the mild double entendre of 'suck.' Not a sophisticated joke but delivered with Monica's characteristic controlling energy. Functional.

dialogue.speaker: Phoebe
dialogue.line: Okay, I know I borrowed some stuff from the Boy Scouts, but that doesn't make my massage oath any less valid. I mean, they have good organizational skills, and I respect that.

jokes.text: Chandler rehearses resisting the gym: 'Don't you want a washboard stomach and rock-hard pecs?' Chandler: 'No, I want a flabby gut and saggy man-breasts.'
jokes.setup: Joey role-plays as the gym's sales pitch; Chandler practices saying no
jokes.punchline: 'No, I want a flabby gut and saggy man-breasts' — delivered as a sincere counter-preference rather than sarcasm
jokes.explanation: 'Saggy man-breasts' is a specifically funny phrase — 'man-breasts' rather than just 'chest' makes it funnier and more self-aware. The deadpan acceptance of an undesirable body is a good Chandler joke. Economy is strong.

dialogue.speaker: Monica
dialogue.line: Is that an ankle bracelet? And your toes are painted?

dialogue.speaker: Phoebe
dialogue.line: Yeah, I'm feet flirting.

dialogue.speaker: Monica
dialogue.line: Feet flirting?

dialogue.speaker: Phoebe
dialogue.line: It's like regular flirting, but with your feet.

jokes.text: Joey: 'That's good.' — approving Chandler's rehearsed answer about wanting saggy man-breasts
jokes.setup: Chandler gives the absurd rehearsed answer about wanting a flabby gut
jokes.punchline: Joey's sincere, coaching approval — 'That's good' — treats this as legitimate preparation
jokes.explanation: A nice reaction beat — Joey takes his coaching role seriously and the brevity of 'That's good' is what makes it work. Depends entirely on delivery and timing.

dialogue.speaker: Phoebe
dialogue.line: Oh, well it was for a thing at work. We had this themed day, right? And it was like, 'Accessories Day,' but it had to be something unconventional. And I was like, 'A toe ring!' And then my boss was like, 'That's not unconventional, Phoebe,' and I was like, 'Well, it is if you're wearing it on your toe!'

jokes.text: Chandler walks into the gym, says 'I want to quit the gym' — the gym employee responds enthusiastically about their new Swedish spa.
jokes.setup: Chandler walks in prepared to quit
jokes.punchline: The gym immediately tries to upsell him on the new Swedish spa, completely ignoring his stated intention
jokes.explanation: The gym subplot is built as a running escalation. The refusal of the gym to engage with Chandler's request is a recognizable real-world frustration played for comedy. Sets up the Maria reveal well.

dialogue.speaker: Monica
dialogue.line: Joey, Rachel cries at everything. She cried at a commercial where a dog wouldn't eat its food because it missed its owner.

jokes.text: Chandler repeats 'I want to quit the gym.' Gym employee: 'Dave in the membership office handles quitters.'
jokes.setup: Chandler tries again to assert his desire to quit
jokes.punchline: 'Dave in the membership office handles quitters' — the word 'quitters' is deployed as a mild, institutional insult
jokes.explanation: The comedy is in the word 'quitters' — treating people who want to leave a gym membership as a shameful category requiring specialized personnel. Good observational comedy about gym culture.

dialogue.speaker: Monica
dialogue.line: You need to apologize to Treeger. You really need to get down on your knees, look him in the eye, and tell him you're sorry.

dialogue.speaker: Joey
dialogue.line: Monica!

dialogue.speaker: Monica
dialogue.line: What? He needs to know you mean it. Really lay it on thick, let it all come out.

jokes.text: Joey is asked if he's a gym member. 'Me? Sorry. Members only.' Joey: 'I want to quit the gym!'
jokes.setup: Joey accompanies Chandler for support; a gym employee mistakes him for wanting membership
jokes.punchline: Joey, caught in the gym's gravitational pull, immediately adopts Chandler's position and also declares he wants to quit
jokes.explanation: The escalation of Chandler's bit to Joey is well-structured. Joey came to help Chandler quit and is now himself trying to quit the gym he just accidentally joined. The structural reversal is clean and funny.

dialogue.speaker: Chandler
dialogue.line: Oh, you know what? You had me at washboard stomach. I'm gonna go back to the gym and sign up right now.

jokes.text: Implied reaction beat: Chandler and Joey are rendered speechless/helpless by Maria. The next dialogue is Phoebe complimenting Rick's feet — suggesting a long, defeated pause at the gym.
jokes.setup: Maria introduces herself to the two men trying to quit the gym
jokes.punchline: The scene cuts away without resolution — implying they utterly failed to resist her
jokes.explanation: The scene transition IS the joke — we don't see their failure, we just know it happened. The gap between Maria saying 'Hi' and the next scene implies total defeat. Good structural comedy.

jokes.text: Phoebe: 'You have really pretty feet.' Rick: 'These old things?'
jokes.setup: Phoebe compliments Rick's feet during the massage
jokes.punchline: Rick's coy, self-deprecating response 'These old things?' — the phrase normally used for clothes/accessories applied to his feet
jokes.explanation: The classic 'these old things?' response applied to feet is a good, economical repurposing of a familiar phrase. Plays well with Phoebe's feet-flirting setup.

dialogue.speaker: Chandler
dialogue.line: I'm quitting! I'm quitting the gym! How can I quit if I can't even get in?!

jokes.text: Rick asks Phoebe to work on his sciatic area. Phoebe: 'You mean... by sciatic, you mean... the towel-covered portion?'
jokes.setup: Rick requests she work on his sciatic area — a legitimate muscle group
jokes.punchline: Phoebe's nervous, halting clarification — 'the towel-covered portion?' — reveals she's interpreting it as a sexual advance (or at least can't separate her attraction from professionalism)
jokes.explanation: 'The towel-covered portion?' is a great phrase — clinical and euphemistic at the same time. The awkward pause implied before it is where the cringe lives. Good Phoebe moment: she's trying to be professional but her attraction keeps breaking through.

dialogue.speaker: Chandler
dialogue.line: Hi, I'm Chandler Bing.

dialogue.speaker: Maria
dialogue.line: Hi.

dialogue.speaker: Chandler
dialogue.line: Could I BE any more attracted to you?

jokes.text: Phoebe asks Rick how he injured the area. Rick: 'A 16-hour sit-in for Greenpeace.'
jokes.setup: Phoebe professionally asks how Rick injured his sciatic area
jokes.punchline: A 16-hour Greenpeace sit-in — absurdly specific, and implies he sat for so long for environmental activism that he hurt his butt
jokes.explanation: The specificity of '16-hour sit-in for Greenpeace' is what makes this land. It establishes Rick as an earnest activist, makes the injury bathetic (you hurt your butt by sitting), and the number '16 hours' adds just the right amount of absurd commitment. Good economy.

jokes.text: Rick: 'Did you just bite me?' Phoebe: 'No!'
jokes.setup: Phoebe is struggling to maintain professional distance while massaging the attractive Rick
jokes.punchline: She clearly did bite him — her denial is instant and unconvincing, implying her attraction literally made her bite a client
jokes.explanation: One of the episode's best jokes. The setup is entirely in what we don't see — the bite happens off-camera (or between lines). Her immediate, unconvincing 'No!' is the perfect non-denial denial. The image of a professional masseuse biting a client she's attracted to is genuinely funny and very Phoebe-specific. Maximum economy — four words, eight syllables total, huge laugh. Comparable to the 8.0 anchor.

dialogue.speaker: Phoebe
dialogue.line: Yeah, I can work on your sciatic area. I'll just... loosen up those muscles.

dialogue.speaker: Phoebe
dialogue.line: Ooh, that's a very... sensitive spot. Very responsive to touch.

dialogue.speaker: Phoebe
dialogue.line: I'm going to apply some pressure here... deep, firm pressure.

jokes.text: Rick: 'Did you just bite me?' / Phoebe: 'No!'
jokes.setup: Phoebe has been losing her battle with attraction; the scene has been building sexual tension through the massage.
jokes.punchline: Phoebe bites her client — the ultimate professional boundary violation — and then immediately denies it.
jokes.explanation: This is the episode's best physical comedy beat. The setup has been building for multiple scenes: the oath, the feet preparation, the 'can I work on the sciatic area' tension. The payoff — biting — is perfectly unexpected yet inevitable. The immediate denial in the face of obvious evidence ('No!') is exactly the right button. Economy is near-perfect: four words, huge laugh. Justifies the 8+ score.

dialogue.speaker: Phoebe
dialogue.line: Oh, your shoulders are so tense. Let me just... work this out for you.

dialogue.speaker: Rick
dialogue.line: That feels great.

dialogue.speaker: Phoebe
dialogue.line: You have such strong arms. I mean, your muscles are just... wow.

dialogue.speaker: Rick
dialogue.line: Thanks. You're a really good masseuse.

dialogue.speaker: Phoebe
dialogue.line: I'm losing my professional composure here...

dialogue.speaker: Phoebe
dialogue.line: *bites him*

dialogue.speaker: Rick
dialogue.line: Ow! Did you just bite me?!

jokes.text: Joey tells Treeger the chick and duck are 'nicknames' — he's the chick and Chandler's the duck. Treeger: 'I would've thought it was the other way around.'
jokes.setup: Joey explains the pets are nicknames; he's the 'chick' and Chandler's the 'duck'
jokes.punchline: Treeger, deadpan, suggests the assignments seem backwards — implying Chandler seems more 'chick-like' and Joey more 'duck-like'
jokes.explanation: Treeger delivers a perfect, economical insult about Chandler's masculinity without spelling it out. The audience fills in the implication. Good use of Treeger as a gruff straight man with unexpected wit.

dialogue.speaker: Treeger
dialogue.line: Wait, you have a chick and a duck?

dialogue.speaker: Joey
dialogue.line: No, no, no. Those are just nicknames.

dialogue.speaker: Treeger
dialogue.line: Nicknames for what?

dialogue.speaker: Joey
dialogue.line: For... Monica and Chandler.

jokes.text: Treeger asks Joey to be his dancing partner. Joey: 'That's not prison lingo, is it?'
jokes.setup: Treeger, as favor for letting the girls stay, asks Joey to be his dancing partner
jokes.punchline: Joey's paranoid check — he wants to confirm 'dancing partner' isn't a prison euphemism — reveals his fear of Treeger and his street-smart paranoia
jokes.explanation: A genuinely funny line. 'That's not prison lingo, is it?' is specific, surprising, and reveals character — Joey is simultaneously relieved they're not being evicted and immediately suspicious of the big intimidating super's request. The line is quotable and has a strong structure.

dialogue.speaker: Treeger
dialogue.line: I hate to break it to you, but I think you got that backwards. You're the duck.

jokes.text: 'I want to quit the gym' — Chandler, appearing out of context in the next scene as a running gag button
jokes.setup: The gym subplot has been running; we cut back to Chandler still at the gym
jokes.punchline: Chandler is still just repeating 'I want to quit the gym' — the sheer futility is the joke
jokes.explanation: The running gag of Chandler flatly repeating his intention to quit gets funnier each time from sheer repetition and futility. By this instance, the phrase itself is the joke.

dialogue.speaker: Joey
dialogue.line: Whoa, whoa, whoa. Mr. Treeger, I'm flattered, but I'm not really into... I mean, I have nothing against it, but I'm just not a dancing partner kind of guy.

dialogue.speaker: Treeger
dialogue.line: What are you talking about? I just need someone to dance with at my nephew's wedding!

dialogue.speaker: Joey
dialogue.line: Oh! ...OH! The dancing! Right, right, right. Yeah, okay, I can do that.

jokes.text: Gym employee asks if Chandler is '100% satisfied with his body.' Chandler: 'Yes. Most of the time. I mean, sure, I have my bad days, but then I remember what a cute smile I have.'
jokes.setup: The gym tries the classic sales tactic — pointing out body dissatisfaction
jokes.punchline: Chandler deflects with genuine self-acceptance anchored to his 'cute smile' — it's sweet, self-deprecating, and undermines the gym's entire pitch
jokes.explanation: A surprisingly layered joke — Chandler's answer is both funny and genuinely sweet. 'I remember what a cute smile I have' is an odd source of self-esteem that simultaneously undermines the gym's tactic. The structure (yes → qualification → 'but then I remember...') is clean.

dialogue.speaker: Monica
dialogue.line: Mr. Treeger asked me to go to the Super Bowl with him.

dialogue.speaker: Monica
dialogue.line: I think he meant the Superintendent's Ball.

jokes.text: Chandler: 'Yes, I hate it here. Everything that you have in here is very heavy.'
jokes.setup: The gym employee asks if Chandler really wants to give up being 'Best-equipped Gym in New York'
jokes.punchline: 'Everything that you have in here is very heavy' — a devastatingly simple, accurate, anti-gym observation
jokes.explanation: A perfect Chandler line. The complaint 'everything in here is very heavy' is simultaneously stupid and completely true — it IS a gym, that's the point. The deadpan obviousness is what makes it brilliant. Great economy.

dialogue.speaker: Joey
dialogue.line: Treeger practices with men because the last time he danced with a woman, he stepped on her foot so hard, they had to amputate it.

dialogue.speaker: Joey
dialogue.line: So now he only dances with men. You know, just to be safe.

jokes.text: Gym employee: 'You want to make your friend work out alone?' Chandler: 'What friend?' Employee: 'Your friend Ross. Just joined.'
jokes.setup: The gym employee tries a new tactic — guilt about a friend
jokes.punchline: Ross has been recruited as a prop in the gym's sales strategy — he 'just joined' to trap Chandler
jokes.explanation: The reveal that the gym has somehow already signed Ross up is a good escalation of the gym's manipulative tactics. The absurdity of the gym as an unstoppable institution is the running joke here.

dialogue.speaker: Ross
dialogue.line: What? What's so funny? I'm getting in shape!

dialogue.speaker: Chandler
dialogue.line: Yeah, that's great, man.

dialogue.speaker: Rachel
dialogue.line: We're just happy for you.

dialogue.speaker: Ross
dialogue.line: No, you're not. You're laughing at me. I can tell.

dialogue.speaker: Chandler
dialogue.line: We would never laugh at you.

dialogue.speaker: Ross
dialogue.line: You're doing it right now!

jokes.text: Joey explains Treeger's situation: he wants to impress 'Marge, this lady super he likes.' Why not practice with a girl? 'He's too shy. He's not good enough to dance with girls yet.'
jokes.setup: Joey explains why Treeger needs a male dance partner
jokes.punchline: 'He's not good enough to dance with girls yet' — as if dancing with girls is an advanced level you graduate to
jokes.explanation: The framing of dancing with women as an achievement to be earned is a funny inversion of normal logic. Joey delivers it with complete sincerity, which is the character-comedy component.

dialogue.speaker: Chandler
dialogue.line: We're never going to quit the gym, are we?

dialogue.speaker: Chandler
dialogue.line: We're going to be 80 years old, still paying for a membership we don't use, still telling ourselves we're going to go tomorrow.

dialogue.speaker: Chandler
dialogue.line: This is my life now. This is who I am. I am a gym member.

jokes.text: Chandler: 'I almost quit. Couldn't leave Ross there without a spotter.' Rachel: 'Wait — so you joined the gym?'
jokes.setup: Chandler returns from the gym mission
jokes.punchline: He not only failed to quit — he accidentally joined (again, it seems, and brought Ross along)
jokes.explanation: Good payoff to the gym subplot. The 'couldn't leave Ross without a spotter' logic is hilariously thin justification for completely failing the mission. Chandler's defeat is total and the audience has earned the laugh.

dialogue.speaker: Ross
dialogue.line: I could close all my bank accounts.

dialogue.speaker: Chandler
dialogue.line: That's your solution? Close your bank accounts?

dialogue.speaker: Ross
dialogue.line: It's the nuclear option.

jokes.text: 'We're doomed. They'll take $50 a month from our accounts for the rest of our lives.'
jokes.setup: Chandler realizes they can't quit the gym conventionally
jokes.punchline: The gym is now framed as a life sentence — '$50 a month for the rest of our lives' delivered with appropriate doom
jokes.explanation: The apocalyptic framing of a gym membership is funny. 'For the rest of our lives' is the right level of dramatic overstatement for Chandler's voice.

dialogue.speaker: Chandler
dialogue.line: Oh no, what am I gonna do? Where am I gonna go to deposit my paycheck and get treated like a criminal?

jokes.text: Chandler's plan: go to the bank, close their accounts, 'cut them off at the source.' Joey: 'You're a genius. Oh, man! But then we won't be bank buddies.'
jokes.setup: Chandler hatches the scheme to close bank accounts to stop gym payments
jokes.punchline: Joey's momentary enthusiasm collapses into grief over losing their 'bank buddy' status — a relationship Joey apparently values highly
jokes.explanation: 'Bank buddies' is a perfectly Joey concept — a made-up designation for a friendship sub-category that only Joey would cherish. His grief is real and immediate, and the concept is novel enough to be memorable. Strong character integration.

dialogue.speaker: Phoebe
dialogue.line: I bit my client.

dialogue.speaker: Monica
dialogue.line: You bit your client?

dialogue.speaker: Phoebe
dialogue.line: On the tushy!

jokes.text: Chandler: 'Now there's two reasons.' (to quit the gym AND close their bank accounts)
jokes.setup: Joey expresses sadness about losing 'bank buddy' status
jokes.punchline: Chandler points out this is now a second reason to go to the bank — not sympathy, just logical accounting
jokes.explanation: A quick, economical tag to the bank buddies joke. Chandler's complete lack of sentimentality about the 'bank buddy' concept is funny in contrast to Joey's devastation. Short and functional.

dialogue.speaker: Phoebe
dialogue.line: I mean, he's got that thing, you know? That thing where you look at him and you just want to... rip his clothes off and lick him like a lollipop.

jokes.text: Phoebe: 'I bit him.' Rachel: 'Where?' Phoebe: 'On the tushy.'
jokes.setup: Phoebe announces she bit her gorgeous client during the massage
jokes.punchline: 'On the tushy' — the location confirms she bit his buttocks, delivered with Phoebe's characteristic gentle vocabulary ('tushy' rather than anything cruder)
jokes.explanation: The payoff to the biting joke. 'On the tushy' is perfect Phoebe vocabulary — the word 'tushy' makes it simultaneously funnier and more innocent, which is exactly Phoebe's register. The structure (setup question, devastating one-word answer) is textbook. One of the episode's standout moments.

dialogue.speaker: Ross
dialogue.line: Sandwiches, baseball, Chandler...

dialogue.speaker: Chandler
dialogue.line: Hey!

jokes.text: Monica: 'And that's not against your oath?' — deadpan reaction to Phoebe biting a client on the tushy
jokes.setup: Phoebe reveals she bit Rick on the tushy during a massage
jokes.punchline: Monica's understated response questions the oath — implying tushy-biting should perhaps be covered by professional codes of conduct
jokes.explanation: A good callback to the oath joke from earlier. Monica's deadpan question ('and that's not against your oath?') treats tushy-biting as a legitimate oath-violation inquiry, which is inherently funny. The callback adds a layer.

dialogue.speaker: Chandler
dialogue.line: Well, thank you. That's exactly what every guy wants to hear.

dialogue.speaker: Ross
dialogue.line: Come on, it works! It's like a visual cold shower.

dialogue.speaker: Chandler
dialogue.line: Yeah, I'm so glad I could help with your... problem.

jokes.text: Phoebe: 'I know, but the moment I touch him, I want to throw out my old oath and take a new, dirty one.'
jokes.setup: Rachel asks if biting violated the oath.
jokes.punchline: 'A new, dirty one' — the contrast between the wholesome Boy Scout oath and a hypothetical 'dirty oath,' combined with Phoebe's total commitment to the framing.
jokes.explanation: Excellent extension of the oath callback. The parallel structure of 'throw out my old oath / take a new, dirty one' is well-crafted. Phoebe framing sexual desire through the formal language of oath-taking is quintessentially her — she treats all moral frameworks with equal seriousness. 'Dirty oath' is an inspired coinage. Earns 8+.

dialogue.speaker: Joey
dialogue.line: What? I'm leading! He's just... his arm's going up my back, and my arm's going around his... wait, how is his other hand on my... that's not possible.

jokes.text: Monica advises Phoebe to think of other things. Ross: 'Like when I'm doing something exciting and I don't want to get too... excited. I try and think of other things. Like sandwiches... and baseball... and Chandler.'
jokes.setup: Monica suggests Phoebe distract herself from attraction; Ross volunteers he does the same thing
jokes.punchline: Ross's distraction list ends with 'Chandler' — implying Chandler is the mental image Ross uses to kill his arousal
jokes.explanation: A brilliant escalating list joke. 'Sandwiches... and baseball...' are expected distraction thoughts. 'And Chandler' is the left-field punchline that implies Chandler is so un-arousing he serves as Ross's arousal-suppression image. The ellipsis structure builds perfectly. Highly quotable and very rewatchable — Chandler's reaction face would make this iconic in the room.

dialogue.speaker: Treeger
dialogue.line: I'm like an anthropomorphic potato out there on the dance floor.

jokes.text: Joey suggests they 'get really drunk' as preparation before dancing with Treeger.
jokes.setup: Treeger asks if they should do some preparation before dancing
jokes.punchline: Joey's suggestion: 'Like get really drunk?' — completely sincere, completely Joey
jokes.explanation: A functional Joey line — getting drunk as dance prep is classically Joey. Not especially original but well-delivered and character-consistent.

dialogue.speaker: Joey
dialogue.line: Hey Chandler, I'm back from dance practice.

dialogue.speaker: Chandler
dialogue.line: How'd it go?

dialogue.speaker: Joey
dialogue.line: Great! I nailed the choreography.

dialogue.speaker: Chandler
dialogue.line: So when are you gonna start doing something about that?

jokes.text: Treeger dancing with Joey — Treeger says Joey's breasts are 'coming out my back' when they try to hold position.
jokes.setup: Joey is dancing as Marge with Treeger, but the position is uncomfortable/wrong
jokes.punchline: 'If I'm Marge, my breasts are coming out my back' — Treeger's complaint implies the dancing is so awkward he's being squeezed uncomfortably
jokes.explanation: A solid physical comedy line — the image of breasts coming out someone's back is absurdly vivid and genuinely funny. The visual comedy here depends on staging but the line works on its own.

dialogue.speaker: Joey
dialogue.line: I'm not dancing, okay? I'm just... moving to the music.

dialogue.speaker: Monica
dialogue.line: Joey, you've been doing the same move for ten minutes.

dialogue.speaker: Joey
dialogue.line: So? That doesn't mean I'm enjoying it.

dialogue.speaker: Monica
dialogue.line: You're literally doing jazz hands right now.

jokes.text: Treeger: 'My mom was right. I'm just a big potato with arms and legs and a head.'
jokes.setup: Treeger gives up in frustration after dancing goes badly
jokes.punchline: 'A big potato with arms and legs and a head' — his mother's devastating description of him, which he has apparently internalized completely
jokes.explanation: The episode's single best joke. 'I'm just a big potato with arms and legs and a head' is perfectly original, devastating, and specific — it's exactly what a cruel mother would say to a large, ungainly son. The specificity of 'a head' (which a potato conspicuously lacks) makes it funnier. The combination of self-deprecation, dark backstory (his mom said this), and the perfect image makes this a genuinely memorable line. Approaches the calibration anchor for a 9+.

dialogue.speaker: Joey
dialogue.line: I did not do that move!

dialogue.speaker: Joey
dialogue.line: That was a... a grand jeté.

jokes.text: Chandler sees Joey dancing with Treeger. Chandler: 'So how goes the dancing? Gay yet?'
jokes.setup: Chandler arrives to find Joey and Treeger in a dance embrace
jokes.punchline: 'Gay yet?' — Chandler's mock concern about the dancing making Joey gay
jokes.explanation: A weak joke by the episode's standards. The 'dancing = gay' joke is lazy and relies on a dated, cheap assumption. Even accounting for the era, it's a crutch — not character-specific (any character could say it), structurally thin, and not original. Below-4 explanation: it's a one-note joke built on a tired premise with no twist or subversion.

dialogue.speaker: Rachel
dialogue.line: Aww, look at you! You're my little disco dancing queen!

jokes.text: Chandler sees Joey doing a little dance step. Joey denies it. Chandler: 'You did a little hop.' Joey: 'And it wasn't a hop. It was a pas de bourrée.'
jokes.setup: Chandler catches Joey doing an involuntary dance move
jokes.punchline: Joey not only knows the specific ballet term but deploys it defensively — revealing he's been secretly learning and enjoying dance
jokes.explanation: Excellent character joke. Joey knowing the technical ballet term 'pas de bourrée' while denying any interest in dancing is a perfect contradiction. The reveal works because it's specific (not just 'it was a dance step' but the actual French term) and Joey delivers it with defensive sincerity. Great character integration — this is exactly how Joey's ego and pride would manifest.

dialogue.speaker: Chandler
dialogue.line: I'm a bank closure specialist? That's not a job, that's a cry for help! I feel like I should be at the gym right now doing reps, not closing banks! Could I BE any more confused about my career?

jokes.text: Chandler: 'You know the words! You are so into this!'
jokes.setup: Joey has just used the ballet term 'pas de bourrée' while denying he enjoys dancing
jokes.punchline: Chandler's delighted call-out — 'You know the words!' — treats the vocabulary as the ultimate betrayal
jokes.explanation: 'You know the words!' is a great follow-on reaction. The idea that knowing dance vocabulary is incriminating is very funny, and Chandler's glee in catching Joey is authentic. Good straight-man work.

dialogue.speaker: Phoebe
dialogue.line: Okay, I'm gonna think of something really unsexy. Um... okay, I'm thinking of Chandler... naked.

dialogue.speaker: Phoebe
dialogue.line: Oh! Oh! Oh my God!

jokes.text: Joey admits he's enjoying dancing: 'Maybe I'm enjoying it a little. I'm getting pretty good at it.'
jokes.setup: Chandler is teasing Joey about clearly enjoying ballroom dancing.
jokes.punchline: Joey's sheepish admission — 'maybe a little' — followed by the proud 'I'm getting pretty good at it' which suggests he's no longer even pretending to just tolerate it.
jokes.explanation: Character pay-off for Joey's arc in this subplot. Not a standalone great joke but serves the story well.

dialogue.speaker: Phoebe
dialogue.line: OK, whenever I start to get excited, I just think of Chandler.

dialogue.speaker: Chandler
dialogue.line: What? Why would that work?

dialogue.speaker: Phoebe
dialogue.line: Well, I think of your weird little body.

dialogue.speaker: Chandler
dialogue.line: Hey!

dialogue.speaker: Phoebe
dialogue.line: Your tiny, narrow shoulders. Your creepy little feet. That thing on your shoulder.

jokes.text: Monica: 'Joey, our little twinkletoes.'
jokes.setup: Joey has just admitted he's enjoying ballroom dancing and getting good at it.
jokes.punchline: 'Twinkletoes' as a nickname — affectionate but emasculating — lands as a sweet button on Joey's transformation.
jokes.explanation: Simple but effective. 'Twinkletoes' does the work in one word. Not a complex joke but appropriate as a button.

dialogue.speaker: Phoebe
dialogue.line: An hour? It felt like a vagina!

jokes.text: Joey demonstrates 'manly' dance moves for the group but immediately admits: 'I don't know how to lead.'
jokes.setup: Joey insists dancing is manly and offers to show manly moves
jokes.punchline: He immediately reveals he's been the follower in all his dance practice — he doesn't know how to lead
jokes.explanation: Good payoff — Joey's masculine posturing collapses the moment he tries to demonstrate. 'I don't know how to lead' is the honest admission that he's been playing the girl's part this whole time, which undercuts everything he just said.

jokes.text: At the bank, Chandler asks to close their accounts. The bank employee refers them to Karen. Chandler: 'I want to quit the bank!'
jokes.setup: At the bank, the same dynamic as the gym begins to emerge — referred to a specialist
jokes.punchline: 'I want to quit the bank!' — the gym joke perfectly transposed to the bank setting
jokes.explanation: The episode's most structurally satisfying callback. The entire gym sequence was setup for this single line — the realization that quitting institutions (gym, bank) works the same manipulative way. 'I want to quit the bank!' is perfectly timed and lands harder than any of the gym iterations because it's the unexpected transposition. Excellent craft.

dialogue.speaker: Mr. Simon
dialogue.line: Oh! I didn't know you two were... I'm so sorry to interrupt!

dialogue.speaker: Mr. Simon
dialogue.line: How much extra would it be for me?

dialogue.speaker: Phoebe
dialogue.line: What? No, no, this isn't—

dialogue.speaker: Mr. Simon
dialogue.line: I have cash. Right now.

jokes.text: Phoebe's distraction attempt: 'Okay, baseball. Rick playing baseball. He slides into second. Maybe even his pants come down a little.'
jokes.setup: Phoebe tries to distract herself from Rick using the suggestions (sandwiches, baseball, Chandler)
jokes.punchline: Her baseball fantasy immediately incorporates Rick — his pants coming down — meaning the distraction is becoming another Rick fantasy
jokes.explanation: A great callback to Ross's advice. Phoebe attempts the prescribed distraction but her fantasy corrupts each one — baseball becomes 'Rick's pants come down a little.' The progression through each failed distraction (sandwiches → baseball → Chandler) with Phoebe's mental commentary is beautifully structured.

dialogue.speaker: Phoebe
dialogue.line: Rick is my husband.

dialogue.speaker: Mrs. Potter
dialogue.line: No, he's not. Rick is married to someone else.

jokes.text: Phoebe: 'Okay, sandwiches. Sandwiches. Okay, on a plate. Maybe Rick's pants come down a little.'
jokes.setup: Phoebe moves to 'sandwiches' as her next distraction after baseball failed
jokes.punchline: Sandwiches also become a Rick fantasy — his pants come down near the sandwiches
jokes.explanation: The escalating corruption of each distraction image is perfectly structured comedy. Sandwiches becoming a Rick-pants-down fantasy is absurd and funny. The repetition of 'Maybe Rick's pants come down a little' as a refrain is the running gag at its best.

dialogue.speaker: Ross
dialogue.line: I'm just going to close my bank account. That way they can't charge me the gym fee.

dialogue.speaker: Chandler
dialogue.line: That's the dumbest thing I've ever heard.

dialogue.speaker: Ross
dialogue.line: Why? It's foolproof!

dialogue.speaker: Monica
dialogue.line: Ross, you need a bank account. You need it for everything.

dialogue.speaker: Ross
dialogue.line: So I'll open a new one.

dialogue.speaker: Phoebe
dialogue.line: But then the gym will just find that one too.

dialogue.speaker: Ross
dialogue.line: Then I'll close that one and open another one.

dialogue.speaker: Rachel
dialogue.line: You'll spend more in fees closing and opening accounts than the gym membership costs.

dialogue.speaker: Ross
dialogue.line: Oh.

jokes.text: Phoebe tries 'Chandler' as the final distraction. 'Chandler. Okay, Chandler. That's working!'
jokes.setup: After baseball and sandwiches both turn into Rick fantasies, Phoebe tries 'Chandler'
jokes.punchline: 'That's working!' — Chandler successfully kills Phoebe's arousal, confirming his role as the group's arousal-suppressor
jokes.explanation: The perfect payoff to Ross's earlier joke about using Chandler to suppress excitement. The callback confirms Chandler's status as the group's universal arousal-killer, and Phoebe's relieved 'That's working!' is the ideal button. The structural integrity (setup joke → failed attempts → payoff) makes this one of the episode's best comedic sequences.

dialogue.speaker: Monica
dialogue.line: So what will we use the joint account for?

dialogue.speaker: Chandler
dialogue.line: Well, you know, joint expenses. Rent, utilities, groceries...

dialogue.speaker: Monica
dialogue.line: Okay, but then how do we track who spent what?

dialogue.speaker: Chandler
dialogue.line: We could keep receipts and divide them up.

dialogue.speaker: Monica
dialogue.line: But then we need a system to organize the receipts.

dialogue.speaker: Chandler
dialogue.line: Right, so we create a spreadsheet.

dialogue.speaker: Monica
dialogue.line: And who maintains the spreadsheet?

dialogue.speaker: Chandler
dialogue.line: We take turns.

dialogue.speaker: Monica
dialogue.line: So now we need a schedule for who maintains it when.

dialogue.speaker: Chandler
dialogue.line: Okay, fine, we'll use a calendar app.

dialogue.speaker: Monica
dialogue.line: Which one? We need to agree on one.

dialogue.speaker: Chandler
dialogue.line: So we're back to needing a joint account just to manage the joint account.

jokes.text: Phoebe's distraction attempts: 'Chandler's knees. Chandler's ankles. Chandler's ankle hair. Oh, no!'
jokes.setup: Chandler as a distraction is working, but Phoebe keeps focusing on specific body parts
jokes.punchline: Working down to 'Chandler's ankle hair' — and then 'Oh, no!' — implying even Chandler's ankle hair has become arousing in the absence of other options, or that she's lost the thread
jokes.explanation: The final escalation in the Chandler distraction sequence. 'Chandler's ankle hair' is a brilliantly specific, absurd detail — ankle hair is both unsexy and very specific, which makes it perfect. The 'Oh, no!' implies the method is failing even at ankle-hair level, suggesting Phoebe may be in worse shape than before. This is a great escalation button.

dialogue.speaker: Phoebe
dialogue.line: So I had the best day today. I found twenty bucks in my old coat pocket, I got to pet a dog, and then I got hit by a bus.

jokes.text: After the massage, Rick: 'I have an enormous crush on you. But since you're a client, I can't ask you out... even though you give me the feelings.'
jokes.setup: The massage ends; Rick confesses his feelings
jokes.punchline: 'Even though you give me the feelings' — the phrase 'the feelings' is a charmingly imprecise euphemism that mirrors Phoebe's own quirky vocabulary
jokes.explanation: A sweet-funny moment. 'You give me the feelings' echoes Phoebe's own eccentric vocabulary — Rick and Phoebe are perfectly matched. Functional but not exceptional.

dialogue.speaker: Phoebe
dialogue.line: I've been fired from every job I've ever had. I was a data processor, then I was a photocopy place girl, then I was a weatherman... I was a brick layer, a sandal maker, a portrait painter... and I was a body double for a celebrity. But you know what? I have never, ever been fired for the same reason twice.

jokes.text: Rick says he'll find another masseuse. Phoebe: 'What?' Rick: 'Yeah, really.' Phoebe: 'What? Suddenly I'm very aware I'm naked.'
jokes.setup: Rick's suggestion he could find another masseuse implies Phoebe would be free to date him
jokes.punchline: 'Suddenly I'm very aware I'm naked' — whether Phoebe means she's vulnerable, excited, or embarrassed, the line is a perfectly timed non-sequitur
jokes.explanation: Wait — Phoebe is the masseuse, so Rick is the naked one. The line 'Suddenly I'm very aware I'm naked' coming from the clothed Phoebe is either a brainfart or an indication of her flustered excitement — which is funnier. The ambiguity and Phoebe's obliviousness make it work. Good economy.

dialogue.speaker: Phoebe
dialogue.line: I'm offering massages on the street.

dialogue.speaker: Phoebe
dialogue.line: No, no, it's just therapeutic massage!

dialogue.speaker: Monica
dialogue.line: Phoebe, people are going to think you're a prostitute.

dialogue.speaker: Phoebe
dialogue.line: Well, I'm not! I'm a masseuse.

jokes.text: Mrs. Potter walks in on Phoebe and Rick apparently in a compromising position. Another employee: 'Why wasn't I offered that? I'd definitely pay more for that.'
jokes.setup: Mrs. Potter walks in and is shocked; the rules of the establishment are invoked
jokes.punchline: A second employee's honest aside — he'd pay extra for whatever he thinks is happening
jokes.explanation: A functional comic beat — the bystander employee's honest market assessment is mildly funny. Not a strong character joke (could be anyone), but it gets a laugh from the awkwardness of the situation.

dialogue.speaker: Phoebe
dialogue.line: Well, I was a prostitute for a while, but I'm not anymore. Whore-wise, I'm doing great.

jokes.text: Phoebe covers: 'Rick is my husband.' Mrs. Potter: 'Oh, really? You'd better tell his other wife. She called three times asking where he is.'
jokes.setup: Phoebe claims Rick is her husband to explain the compromising situation
jokes.punchline: Mrs. Potter reveals Rick actually has a wife who has been calling — making Rick a married man who was flirting with his masseuse
jokes.explanation: A good escalating reveal — Rick is not just taken, he's married, and his wife has been frantically calling. The 'three times' detail adds specificity. Good structural subversion of Phoebe's attempted cover story.

dialogue.speaker: Joey
dialogue.line: Hey Treeger, from now on I'm gonna call you 'Chick'.

dialogue.speaker: Treeger
dialogue.line: Chick? Why Chick?

dialogue.speaker: Joey
dialogue.line: Well, you call me Duck, I call you Chick. We're both birds, man.

jokes.text: Phoebe: 'Yes, I will tell her.' — responding to Mrs. Potter saying she should tell Rick's other wife
jokes.setup: Mrs. Potter says Phoebe should tell Rick's wife about the affair
jokes.punchline: Phoebe agrees earnestly — 'Yes, I will tell her' — as if she's a neutral party accepting a task, not the person who was making out with the husband
jokes.explanation: Phoebe's earnest acceptance of the task ('Yes, I will tell her') is perfectly in character — she processes the situation and takes on the responsibility with complete sincerity despite being the one who caused the problem. Good character integration.

dialogue.speaker: Joey
dialogue.line: Yeah! We nailed it! We absolutely nailed it!

dialogue.speaker: Treeger
dialogue.line: We sure did.

dialogue.speaker: Joey
dialogue.line: I'm gonna go home and practice some more moves on Chandler.

jokes.text: Chandler: 'So you didn't leave the bank?' Joey: 'And somehow we ended up with a joint checking account.'
jokes.setup: The bank visit was supposed to close their accounts
jokes.punchline: They didn't close accounts — they opened a new one together — a joint checking account, which is somehow worse than what they started with
jokes.explanation: The perfect payoff to the bank subplot — they went to close accounts and accidentally opened a joint account. The 'somehow' in Joey's delivery is the key word — it implies they know they failed but can't quite explain how. Excellent structural comedy.

dialogue.speaker: Joey
dialogue.line: Come on, Mr. Treeger, let's run through that routine one more time.

dialogue.speaker: Treeger
dialogue.line: You know what, Joey? I'm feeling pretty good about myself these days.

dialogue.speaker: Joey
dialogue.line: Yeah? That's great, Mr. Treeger!

dialogue.speaker: Treeger
dialogue.line: I mean, I'm out there, I'm dancing, I'm meeting people. I feel like I can do anything now.

dialogue.speaker: Joey
dialogue.line: That's exactly what I wanted to hear, man.

dialogue.speaker: Treeger
dialogue.line: You know, I think I've finally figured out who I am.

jokes.text: Chandler: 'What will you ever use that for?' Joey: 'To pay for the gym.'
jokes.setup: Chandler asks what they'll use the joint account for
jokes.punchline: 'To pay for the gym' — the gym and bank subplots are now permanently linked; the gym has won
jokes.explanation: The episode's most satisfying structural payoff. Four words that close both the gym AND bank subplots while delivering a final, conclusive defeat. The gym has beat them completely: they didn't quit, they failed to close their accounts, and now they have a JOINT account specifically designated for gym payments. Exceptional economy and structure — this is textbook sitcom subplot resolution through comedy.

dialogue.speaker: Treeger
dialogue.line: I'm taking Marge's friend to the dance.

dialogue.speaker: Joey
dialogue.line: That's great, Treeger!

dialogue.speaker: Treeger
dialogue.line: Yeah, well, you know, she's about my size. That way we'll move together real nice.

jokes.text: Phoebe reports: 'Rick and I hit it off. We were making out. Then my boss walked in and fired me for being a whore.'
jokes.setup: Phoebe updates the group on her day
jokes.punchline: 'Fired me for being a whore' — Phoebe uses the word matter-of-factly, as if reporting neutral information
jokes.explanation: Phoebe's deadpan delivery of her own firing 'for being a whore' is very funny — the word is shocking coming from Phoebe, which is the joke. Her matter-of-fact tone suggests she's accepted the characterization with equanimity, which is classic Phoebe.

dialogue.speaker: Interviewer
dialogue.line: So why did you leave your last job?

dialogue.speaker: Phoebe
dialogue.line: Oh, my boss was stealing from the register, so I had to kill him.

jokes.text: Phoebe: 'It's so weird. I have never been fired from anything.'
jokes.setup: The group reacts to Phoebe being fired
jokes.punchline: Phoebe's surprise is that she's never been fired before — not that she was fired for being 'a whore.' The wrong detail is remarkable to her.
jokes.explanation: Phoebe's sense of priorities is wrong in exactly the right way. The transgression she focuses on is that she was fired — not the context. Good character comedy that plays on Phoebe's obliviousness to the gravity of some situations.

jokes.text: Phoebe: 'I started walking around, not knowing what to do next. I started asking people on the street if they wanted massages.'
jokes.setup: Phoebe explains what she did after being fired
jokes.punchline: She started soliciting strangers on the street for massages — which, given the context of just being called a whore, reads as darkly ironic
jokes.explanation: The irony of Phoebe, freshly fired for 'being a whore,' immediately taking her services to the street is dark and funny. Phoebe's complete obliviousness to how this looks is perfect character comedy.

jokes.text: Phoebe: 'Then these policemen thought I was a whore too. It's really been a bad day, whore-wise.'
jokes.setup: Phoebe explains that after soliciting on the street, she was approached by police
jokes.punchline: 'It's really been a bad day, whore-wise' — the phrase 'whore-wise' is perfect Phoebe: she categorizes this as a classification problem, not a behavior problem
jokes.explanation: The episode's best line. 'Whore-wise' is a perfect, original, hilarious coinage that could only come from Phoebe. The construction ('it's been a bad day, [noun]-wise') is a familiar language pattern repurposed with a shocking word. Phoebe's framing — that her day has been specifically bad in the 'whore' category, as if this is a metric she tracks — is brilliant. Maximum economy, maximum character specificity, deeply original. Approaches the calibration anchor for a legendary line.

jokes.text: Chandler calls Joey 'Duck,' then corrects himself when addressed: 'Yeah, Bunny Rabbit.'
jokes.setup: Treeger established earlier that he thought the chick/duck nicknames were backwards; Chandler addresses Joey as 'Duck'
jokes.punchline: When Joey (as Chick) calls Chandler 'Duck,' Chandler confirms with 'Yeah, Bunny Rabbit' — a completely new nickname that makes no sense
jokes.explanation: A callback to the earlier chick/duck nickname joke. 'Bunny Rabbit' as a self-applied nickname is a mild absurdist gag. The callback is a bit loose — it mostly functions as scene atmosphere.

jokes.text: After Treeger leaves for the ball, Joey: 'Good luck. Unless you want to practice the fox trot? Or the tango?'
jokes.setup: Joey sends Treeger off with good wishes
jokes.punchline: Joey immediately offers to keep dancing — revealing he's now genuinely hooked on dancing and doesn't want to stop
jokes.explanation: A good character beat — Joey's arc in the episode is completed here. He went from reluctant practice partner to genuinely hooked dancer. The casual mention of 'fox trot? Or the tango?' implies he's learned multiple dances. Character growth delivered through comedy.

jokes.text: Treeger: 'You'd dance good with her. She's the same size as me.' Joey declines.
jokes.setup: Treeger offers to set Joey up with Marge's friend at the dance
jokes.punchline: The selling point is that the woman is 'the same size as me' — i.e., a large woman — which is Treeger's idea of a compliment to Joey's dance skills
jokes.explanation: A mild character joke — Treeger's attempt at matchmaking is inadvertently insulting. Works as a character beat but isn't particularly sharp. Functions well as an episode coda.

jokes.text: Phoebe at a job interview. Interviewer: 'Reason for leaving last job?' Phoebe: 'They thought I was a whore.'
jokes.setup: Phoebe is at a job interview; standard question about reason for leaving last job
jokes.punchline: 'They thought I was a whore' — Phoebe gives the literal, honest answer with no filter or reframing
jokes.explanation: A superb cold-close joke. The job interview context makes Phoebe's literal honesty devastating — she gives the factually accurate answer ('they thought I was a whore') with complete professional sincerity. The callback to her firing works perfectly as a closer. The interviewer's response ('Okay. We'll give you a call if anything comes up') is a perfect deadpan tag. One of the episode's top moments.

jokes.text: Interviewer: 'Okay. We'll give you a call if anything comes up.' Phoebe: 'Great. Thank you very much.'
jokes.setup: Phoebe has just told a job interviewer her reason for leaving was 'they thought I was a whore'
jokes.punchline: The interviewer gives the standard, non-committal interview close — as if this is a normal answer. Phoebe thanks him professionally.
jokes.explanation: The straight-man interviewer's deadpan 'We'll give you a call if anything comes up' is the perfect tag to the job interview scene. His professionalism in the face of Phoebe's disclosure is the joke — the scene ends without anyone acknowledging how absurd the exchange was. Great button.

tmdb_overview: Joey attempts ballroom dancing in order to help Monica and Rachel keep their illegal sublet. Phoebe is attracted to one of her massage clients. And Ross tries to help Chandler quit the gym.
insight: Uneven pacing undermines 69 jokes; character comedy carries a middling 67.6 score.
